notes:
1. South Indian History — Scope

  • South Indian history developed through interaction among the regions of present-day:
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Kerala.
  • Karnataka.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
  • Important political traditions included:
  • Cheras.
  • Cholas.
  • Pandyas.
  • Pallavas.
  • Chalukyas.
  • Rashtrakutas.
  • Hoysalas.
  • Kakatiyas.
  • Yadavas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

South Indian History → Dynasties + Temples + Trade + Literature + Local Administration

2. Geographical Background

Major physical features influencing South Indian history included:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Deccan Plateau.
  • Kaveri basin.
  • Krishna basin.
  • Godavari basin.
  • Coromandel Coast.
  • Malabar Coast.

3. Rivers and Political Centres

Important river valleys supported powerful kingdoms:

  • Kaveri → Cholas.
  • Vaigai → Pandyas.
  • Krishna–Tungabhadra → Chalukyas and later powers.
  • Periyar and western rivers → Chera/Kerala regions.

4. Maritime Advantage

The long coastline encouraged trade with:

  • Sri Lanka.
  • Southeast Asia.
  • Arabian Peninsula.
  • Roman Mediterranean world.
  • China.

5. Sangam-Age Three Crowned Kings

The three major Tamil dynasties were known as the Muvendar:

  • Chera.
  • Chola.
  • Pandya.
📌 Must-Memorise

Muvendar → Chera + Chola + Pandya

6. Sangam Literature

Important Sangam collections include:

  • Ettuthokai.
  • Pattuppattu.

They contain valuable information on:

  • Kings.
  • Warfare.
  • Trade.
  • Society.
  • Landscapes.

7. Tolkappiyam

  • Tolkappiyam is the earliest surviving Tamil grammatical work.
  • It also provides information about:
  • Society.
  • Poetics.
  • Landscapes.
  • Cultural life.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tolkappiyam → Early Tamil Grammar

8. Sangam Landscape Classification

The five major landscapes were:

  • Kurinji.
  • Mullai.
  • Marutham.
  • Neithal.
  • Palai.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kurinji → Hills

Mullai → Pastoral

Marutham → Agricultural Plains

Neithal → Coast

Palai → Arid Zone

9. Early Cheras

  • Early Chera rulers controlled parts of:
  • Western Tamil region.
  • Kerala.
  • Their power was closely linked with western coastal trade.

10. Chera Emblem

  • The traditional emblem of the Cheras was the bow.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chera → Bow

11. Chola Emblem

  • The traditional emblem of the Cholas was the tiger.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chola → Tiger

12. Pandya Emblem

  • The traditional emblem of the Pandyas was the fish.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pandya → Fish

13. Early Chera Capital

  • Vanji is traditionally associated with the Chera capital.
  • Its precise archaeological identification remains debated.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Vanji → Chera Capital Tradition; Exact Location Debated

14. Chera Ports

Important Chera-associated ports included:

  • Muziris.
  • Tondi.

15. Muziris

  • Muziris was a major west-coast port connected with Roman and Indian Ocean trade.
  • It is generally associated with the Kodungallur region of Kerala.
📌 Must-Memorise

Muziris → Chera Trade → Kerala Coast

16. Senguttuvan

  • Cheran Senguttuvan was one of the most famous Chera rulers.
  • He is celebrated in Tamil literary tradition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Senguttuvan → Chera

17. Pattini Tradition

  • Senguttuvan is associated with the Pattini/Kannagi cult in later literary tradition.
  • Silappadikaram connects him with the consecration of Kannagi.

18. Early Cholas

  • Early Chola territory centred on the fertile Kaveri basin.
  • Important political centres included:
  • Uraiyur.
  • Kaveripattinam/Puhar.

19. Uraiyur

  • Uraiyur, near present-day Tiruchirappalli, was an important early Chola centre.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Uraiyur → Early Chola Centre

20. Puhar

  • Kaveripattinam, also called Puhar, was a major Chola port.
  • It was located near the mouth of the Kaveri.
📌 Must-Memorise

Puhar → Kaveripattinam → Chola Port

21. Karikala Chola

  • Karikala was the most famous early Chola ruler.
  • Sangam traditions associate him with:
  • Military victories.
  • Kaveri irrigation.
  • Development of Puhar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Karikala → Early Chola

22. Battle of Venni

  • Karikala is traditionally associated with victory at the Battle of Venni.
  • The battle strengthened his position among Tamil rulers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Venni → Karikala Chola

23. Kallanai

  • Karikala is traditionally credited with construction or major development of the Kallanai across the Kaveri.
  • Kallanai is also known as the Grand Anicut.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kallanai → Karikala → Kaveri

24. Importance of Kallanai

Kallanai helped:

  • Divert Kaveri water.
  • Support irrigation.
  • Expand agriculture in the delta.

25. Early Pandyas

  • Early Pandya power centred on:
  • Madurai.
  • Vaigai basin.
  • They were active in inland and maritime trade.

26. Pandya Capital

  • Madurai was the principal political and cultural centre of the Pandyas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pandya Capital → Madurai

27. Korkai

  • Korkai was an important ancient Pandya port.
  • It was famous for pearl fisheries.
📌 Must-Memorise

Korkai → Pandya → Pearls

28. Pearl Fishery

  • Gulf of Mannar waters were famous for pearls.
  • Pearl fishing contributed to Pandya wealth and international trade.

29. Roman Trade with Tamilakam

Evidence includes:

  • Roman coins.
  • Amphora fragments.
  • Imported ceramics.
  • Literary references.

30. Yavana

  • Tamil literature uses the term Yavana for western foreigners, often Greeks or Romans in early historic contexts.

31. Arikamedu

  • Arikamedu near Puducherry is an important archaeological site associated with Indo-Roman trade.
📌 Must-Memorise

Arikamedu → Indo-Roman Trade

32. Roman Coin Finds

Roman coins have been found in several parts of South India, including Tamil Nadu, showing extensive trade links.

33. Main Exports from South India

Exports included:

  • Pepper.
  • Pearls.
  • Ivory.
  • Precious stones.
  • Textiles.
  • Spices.

34. Imports

Imports included:

  • Gold.
  • Wine.
  • Glassware.
  • Luxury goods.

35. Kalabhra Period

  • After the early historic Tamil dynasties, the Kalabhras became influential in Tamil country.
  • Their period is usually placed broadly between the decline of the Sangam polities and the rise of Pallavas and later Pandyas.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Kalabhra Period → Poorly Documented; Avoid Calling It Simply a "Dark Age"

36. Kalabhra Sources

Knowledge comes mainly from:

  • Later inscriptions.
  • Literary references.
  • Religious traditions.

Their exact origin remains uncertain.

37. Religious Developments During Kalabhra Period

  • Jainism and Buddhism continued to be influential.
  • Tamil literary activity also continued.

38. Pallavas

  • Pallavas emerged as a major power in northern Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra regions.
  • Their important capital was Kanchipuram.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pallava Capital → Kanchipuram

39. Pallava Political Region

Pallava power was centred in:

  • Tondaimandalam.
  • Northern Tamil Nadu.
  • Southern Andhra region.

40. Early Pallava Records

  • Early Pallava inscriptions were issued in:
  • Prakrit.
  • Later Sanskrit.
  • Tamil became increasingly important in local records.

41. Simhavishnu

  • Simhavishnu was an important Pallava ruler.
  • He expanded Pallava authority southward.
  • He laid foundations for later imperial Pallava power.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simhavishnu → Early Imperial Pallava Expansion

42. Mahendravarman I

  • Mahendravarman I ruled in the early seventh century.
  • He was:
  • Ruler.
  • Patron of architecture.
  • Literary figure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahendravarman I → Rock-Cut Architecture

43. Mahendravarman and Religion

  • Tradition holds that Mahendravarman initially patronised Jainism and later became associated with Shaivism.
  • Appar is connected with this religious transition in Shaiva tradition.

44. Appar

  • Appar, also known as Tirunavukkarasar, was one of the great Shaiva Nayanmars.
  • He was active during the Pallava period.

45. Mandagapattu Inscription

  • The Mandagapattu inscription of Mahendravarman I is famous in architectural history.
  • It refers to a temple constructed without:
  • Brick.
  • Timber.
  • Metal.
  • Mortar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mandagapattu → Mahendravarman I

46. Rock-Cut Temples

Mahendravarman patronised rock-cut cave temples at places such as:

  • Mandagapattu.
  • Mamandur.
  • Mahendravadi.
  • Dalavanur.

47. Mattavilasa Prahasana

  • Mahendravarman I wrote the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mattavilasa Prahasana → Mahendravarman I

48. Chalukya–Pallava Conflict

  • The Pallavas and Badami Chalukyas fought repeatedly for supremacy in the southern Deccan and Tamil regions.
  • Their rivalry became one of the major political struggles of the seventh century.

49. Pulakeshin II

  • Pulakeshin II was the greatest ruler of the Badami Chalukyas.
  • He defeated Mahendravarman I and advanced into Pallava territory.

50. Narasimhavarman I

  • Narasimhavarman I succeeded Mahendravarman I.
  • He became one of the greatest Pallava rulers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Narasimhavarman I → Mamalla

51. Mamalla

  • Narasimhavarman I bore the title Mamalla, meaning great wrestler.
  • Mamallapuram is associated with his title.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mamalla → Narasimhavarman I

Mamallapuram → Mamalla

52. Battle Against Pulakeshin II

  • Narasimhavarman I defeated the Chalukyas.
  • Pallava forces captured Vatapi, the Chalukya capital, around 642 CE.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vatapi Captured → Narasimhavarman I

53. Vatapikonda

  • Narasimhavarman I assumed the title Vatapikonda after capturing Vatapi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vatapikonda → Narasimhavarman I

54. Vatapi

  • Vatapi is the ancient name of present-day Badami in Karnataka.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vatapi = Badami

55. Paranjothi

  • Pallava general Paranjothi is traditionally associated with the Vatapi campaign.
  • Shaiva tradition later identifies him with the saint Siruthondar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paranjothi → Vatapi Campaign → Siruthondar Tradition

56. Hiuen Tsang and Kanchipuram

  • Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang/Hiuen Tsang visited Kanchipuram in the seventh century.
  • He described it as an important centre of learning and religion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Xuanzang → Kanchipuram → Pallava Period

57. Mamallapuram

  • Mamallapuram, also called Mahabalipuram, was an important Pallava port and monumental centre.
  • It lies on the Coromandel Coast.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mamallapuram → Pallavas

58. Pancha Rathas

  • The Pancha Rathas at Mamallapuram are monolithic rock-cut monuments.
  • They are popularly named after the Pandavas and Draupadi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pancha Rathas → Mamallapuram → Pallava

59. Monolithic Architecture

  • Each ratha was carved from a single mass of rock.
  • They experiment with different temple forms.

60. Descent of the Ganges / Arjuna's Penance

  • The huge open-air relief at Mamallapuram is interpreted as either:
  • Descent of the Ganges.
  • Arjuna's Penance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Great Open-Air Relief → Mamallapuram

61. Narasimhavarman II

  • Narasimhavarman II is also known as Rajasimha.
  • He was an important later Pallava ruler.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajasimha → Narasimhavarman II

62. Structural Temple Phase

  • Under later Pallavas, architecture shifted increasingly from rock-cut monuments to structural stone temples.

63. Shore Temple

  • Shore Temple at Mamallapuram was built under Narasimhavarman II/Rajasimha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shore Temple → Rajasimha → Mamallapuram

64. Kailasanatha Temple

  • Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram was built under Rajasimha.
  • It is one of the earliest major structural temples of Tamil Nadu.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kailasanatha Temple → Kanchipuram → Rajasimha

65. Nandivarman II

  • Nandivarman II, also called Pallavamalla, became ruler after a succession crisis.
  • His reign saw renewed warfare with Chalukyas and Pandyas.

66. Vaikuntha Perumal Temple

  • Vaikuntha Perumal Temple at Kanchipuram is associated with Nandivarman II.
  • Its sculptures provide valuable dynastic and historical information.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vaikuntha Perumal → Nandivarman II

67. Pallava Architecture — Three Stages

Broadly:

  • Mahendra style → Rock-cut caves.
  • Mamalla style → Monolithic rathas and reliefs.
  • Rajasimha style → Structural temples.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahendra → Caves

Mamalla → Rathas

Rajasimha → Structural Temples

68. Pallava Administration

Administrative divisions included terms such as:

  • Kottam.
  • Nadu.
  • Ur.

69. Kottam

  • Kottam was an important territorial division in Pallava country.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pallava Region → Kottam

70. Brahmadeya

  • Brahmadeya referred to tax-privileged land grants to Brahmanas.
  • Such settlements became important centres of agricultural expansion.

71. Sabha

  • Sabha was an assembly associated mainly with Brahmana villages.

72. Ur

  • Ur was the general village assembly in many non-Brahmana settlements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sabha → Brahmadeya Village

Ur → General Village

73. Nagaram

  • Nagaram referred to an organisation of merchants or urban commercial community.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nagaram → Merchant Organisation

74. Pallava Religion

Pallava rulers patronised:

  • Shaivism.
  • Vaishnavism.
  • Jainism.
  • Buddhism in certain periods.

75. Bhakti Movement

The Pallava period witnessed the growth of Tamil Bhakti traditions represented by:

  • Nayanmars.
  • Alvars.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nayanmars → Shaiva

Alvars → Vaishnava

76. Tevaram

  • Tevaram hymns are associated principally with:
  • Appar.
  • Sambandar.
  • Sundarar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tevaram → Appar + Sambandar + Sundarar

77. Nalayira Divya Prabandham

  • The Nalayira Divya Prabandham is the collection of Tamil Vaishnava hymns of the Alvars.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alvars → Nalayira Divya Prabandham

78. Andal

  • Andal was the only woman among the twelve Alvars.
  • She is associated with:
  • Tiruppavai.
  • Nachiyar Tirumoli.
📌 Must-Memorise

Andal → Tiruppavai

79. Badami Chalukyas

  • The Early Western Chalukyas, commonly called Badami Chalukyas, ruled much of the Deccan.
  • Their capital was Vatapi/Badami.
📌 Must-Memorise

Badami Chalukya Capital → Vatapi

80. Founder of Badami Chalukya Power

  • Pulakeshin I established Badami as a fortified capital.
  • Later rulers greatly expanded Chalukya power.

81. Pulakeshin II

  • Pulakeshin II was the greatest Badami Chalukya ruler.
  • His reign is known especially from the Aihole inscription.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pulakeshin II → Aihole Inscription

82. Aihole Inscription

  • The Aihole inscription was composed by Ravikirti.
  • It praises Pulakeshin II.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aihole Inscription → Ravikirti → Pulakeshin II

83. Harsha vs Pulakeshin II

  • Pulakeshin II defeated or checked Harshavardhana on the Narmada frontier.
  • This prevented Harsha's expansion deep into the Deccan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pulakeshin II → Checked Harsha

84. Narmada

  • The Narmada became an important political boundary between Harsha's northern sphere and Chalukya power.

85. Xuanzang and Pulakeshin II

  • Xuanzang described the Chalukya kingdom and Pulakeshin II's power.

86. Eastern Chalukyas

  • Pulakeshin II established his brother Vishnuvardhana in the eastern Deccan.
  • This led to the Eastern Chalukya dynasty of Vengi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eastern Chalukyas → Vengi → Vishnuvardhana

87. Vengi

  • Vengi lay in the fertile Krishna-Godavari delta region.
  • It became strategically important in later Chola politics.

88. Chalukya Architecture

Important centres include:

  • Aihole.
  • Badami.
  • Pattadakal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chalukya Architecture → Aihole + Badami + Pattadakal

89. Aihole

  • Aihole contains numerous early structural temples.
  • It is often called an architectural laboratory because of experiments with different temple forms.

90. Badami Cave Temples

  • Badami contains rock-cut cave temples dedicated to:
  • Hindu deities.
  • Jain traditions.

91. Pattadakal

  • Pattadakal contains temples combining northern and southern architectural forms.
  • It served as an important Chalukya ceremonial centre.

92. Virupaksha Temple, Pattadakal

  • The Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal was commissioned by Queen Lokamahadevi.
  • It commemorated Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Virupaksha Temple, Pattadakal → Lokamahadevi

93. Rashtrakutas

  • Rashtrakutas replaced the Badami Chalukyas as the dominant Deccan power in the eighth century.
  • Their major capital was Manyakheta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rashtrakuta Capital → Manyakheta

94. Founder of Rashtrakuta Imperial Power

  • Dantidurga established Rashtrakuta imperial power in the Deccan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dantidurga → Rashtrakuta

95. Krishna I

  • Krishna I was an important Rashtrakuta ruler.
  • He is famous for commissioning the Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kailasanatha Temple, Ellora → Krishna I

96. Kailasanatha at Ellora

  • It is a massive monolithic rock-cut temple dedicated to Shiva.
  • It was carved downward from a single rock mass.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ellora Kailasa → Monolithic → Rashtrakuta

97. Dhruva

  • Dhruva Dharavarsha expanded Rashtrakuta power into northern India.

98. Govinda III

  • Govinda III extended Rashtrakuta influence over a vast region.
  • He participated in struggles for northern supremacy.

99. Tripartite Struggle

The Tripartite Struggle involved:

  • Rashtrakutas.
  • Gurjara-Pratiharas.
  • Palas.

They competed for control of Kannauj.

📌 Must-Memorise

Tripartite Struggle → Pala + Pratihara + Rashtrakuta

100. Amoghavarsha I

  • Amoghavarsha I was one of the longest-ruling Rashtrakuta kings.
  • He was known for:
  • Literature.
  • Religious patronage.
  • Cultural interests.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amoghavarsha → Rashtrakuta Cultural Patron

101. Kavirajamarga

  • Kavirajamarga is one of the earliest major works on Kannada poetics and literature.
  • It is associated with Amoghavarsha I's court.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kavirajamarga → Amoghavarsha Period → Kannada

102. Jainism Under Rashtrakutas

  • Rashtrakutas patronised Jain scholars as well as Hindu institutions.
  • Jain literature flourished in Kannada and Sanskrit.

103. Rashtrakuta Religious Tolerance

Royal patronage extended to:

  • Shaivism.
  • Vaishnavism.
  • Jainism.

104. Later Western Chalukyas

  • The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani rose after Rashtrakuta decline.
  • Their capital was Kalyani, present-day Basavakalyan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kalyani Chalukyas → Kalyani / Basavakalyan

105. Tailapa II

  • Tailapa II overthrew Rashtrakuta power and established the Western Chalukya dynasty of Kalyani.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tailapa II → Kalyani Chalukya Founder

106. Western Chalukya–Chola Rivalry

  • Cholas and Western Chalukyas fought repeatedly over:
  • Vengi.
  • Tungabhadra region.
  • Eastern Deccan succession politics.

107. Chola Revival

  • Chola imperial power revived in the ninth century under Vijayalaya Chola.
  • He captured Thanjavur and established a strong base in the Kaveri region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Imperial Chola Founder → Vijayalaya Chola

108. Vijayalaya Chola

  • Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur around the middle of the ninth century.
  • He established the later Imperial Chola dynasty.

109. Nishumbhasudani Temple

  • Vijayalaya is traditionally associated with the construction of a temple to Nishumbhasudani at Thanjavur.

110. Aditya I

  • Aditya I expanded Chola power.
  • He defeated the Pallavas and brought much of Tondaimandalam under Chola control.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aditya I → End of Pallava Political Supremacy

111. Parantaka I

  • Parantaka I ruled for several decades.
  • He expanded into Pandya territory.
  • He used titles reflecting victory over Madurai.

112. Battle of Takkolam

  • The Cholas suffered a major defeat at Takkolam against Rashtrakuta forces in 949 CE.
  • Chola prince Rajaditya was killed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Takkolam → 949 → Rashtrakutas Defeated Cholas

113. Rajaraja I

  • Rajaraja I ruled from 985 to 1014 CE.
  • He transformed the Chola kingdom into a major imperial power.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajaraja I → 985–1014

114. Rajaraja's Birth Name

  • Rajaraja I was originally named Arulmozhi Varman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Arulmozhi Varman → Rajaraja I

115. Rajaraja's Conquests

He expanded into:

  • Pandya country.
  • Kerala regions.
  • Northern Sri Lanka.
  • Parts of Karnataka.
  • Maldives.

116. Kandalur Salai

  • Rajaraja's inscriptions refer to his action at Kandalur Salai.
  • It is traditionally interpreted as an important early military/naval achievement against Chera-linked power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kandalur Salai → Rajaraja I

117. Sri Lanka

  • Rajaraja conquered northern parts of Sri Lanka.
  • Anuradhapura was attacked and Chola authority extended into the island.

118. Maldives

  • Chola inscriptions associate Rajaraja with conquest of islands identified with the Maldives.

119. Thanjavur

  • Thanjavur became a major imperial Chola capital.
  • Rajaraja constructed the Brihadisvara Temple there.

120. Brihadisvara Temple

  • Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur was completed around 1010 CE.
  • It is dedicated to Shiva.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Brihadisvara Temple → Rajaraja I → 1010 CE

121. Rajarajesvaram

  • Brihadisvara Temple was originally called Rajarajesvaram after Rajaraja I.

122. Chola Temple Architecture

Key features include:

  • Massive vimana.
  • Axial planning.
  • Sculptural decoration.
  • Inscriptions.
  • Temple economy.

123. Vimana

  • Vimana is the tower rising above the sanctum of a South Indian temple.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Vimana → Above Sanctum

Gopuram → Entrance Gateway

124. Rajaraja's Inscriptions

  • Brihadisvara Temple contains extensive inscriptions recording:
  • Donations.
  • Temple staff.
  • Land.
  • Jewellery.
  • Ritual arrangements.

125. Rajendra I

  • Rajendra I succeeded Rajaraja I.
  • He ruled from 1012/1014 to 1044 and greatly expanded Chola power.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajendra I → Son and Successor of Rajaraja I

126. Ganga Campaign

  • Rajendra I conducted a northern campaign reaching the Ganga region.
  • He adopted the title Gangaikonda Chola.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gangaikonda Chola → Rajendra I

127. Gangaikonda Cholapuram

  • Rajendra I founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram as a new imperial capital.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gangaikonda Cholapuram → Rajendra I

128. Temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram

  • Rajendra built a great Shiva temple there inspired by, but distinct from, Brihadisvara at Thanjavur.

129. Kadaram Expedition

  • Rajendra I launched a naval expedition against the Srivijaya kingdom in Southeast Asia in 1025 CE.
  • Kadaram is usually identified with Kedah in the Malay Peninsula.
📌 Must-Memorise

1025 → Rajendra I → Srivijaya / Kadaram

130. Reason for Srivijaya Campaign

Possible motives included:

  • Control of maritime trade routes.
  • Commercial rivalry.
  • Political prestige.

131. Chola Navy

  • Cholas possessed significant naval capacity.
  • It was used against:
  • Sri Lanka.
  • Maldives.
  • Southeast Asian targets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chola Naval Power → Rajaraja I + Rajendra I

132. Chola–China Trade

  • Chola-period merchant missions reached Song China.
  • South Indian trade formed part of the wider Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean economy.

133. Rajadhiraja I

  • Rajadhiraja I continued Chola campaigns against:
  • Western Chalukyas.
  • Sri Lanka.
  • Pandyas.

134. Battle of Koppam

  • Rajadhiraja I died fighting the Western Chalukyas at Koppam in 1054.
  • Rajendra II continued the battle and claimed victory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Koppam → Rajadhiraja I Killed

135. Kulottunga I

  • Kulottunga I came from the Eastern Chalukya-Chola line.
  • He became Chola emperor in 1070.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kulottunga I → Chalukya-Chola Line

136. Chola–Eastern Chalukya Link
